title: Italia visa. Charybdis. Aetna. Naufragus
titleEn: Italy Sighted, Charybdis, Etna and the Castaway — Aeneid III.506–612
part: Italy Sighted, Charybdis, Etna and the Castaway (III.506–612)
about: The fleet leaves Epirus by the Ceraunian cliffs, where the sea-crossing to Italy is shortest, and beaches for the night. While the crews sleep, the helmsman Palinurus rises, reads the winds and the gliding stars, and gives the signal to sail. At dawn Achates is the first to cry out that Italy lies ahead, and the whole company echoes him. Anchises crowns a mixing-bowl with a garland, fills it with wine, and standing on the high stern prays to the gods of sea, land and storm for a fair wind. They come to a harbour with a temple of Minerva on the height, and there Aeneas sees four white horses grazing: an omen. Anchises reads it twice over, as war, since horses are armed for war, and as hope of peace, since these same beasts are trained to the yoke. They pray to Pallas and, as Helenus had taught them, sacrifice to Argive Juno with heads veiled, then leave the Greek-settled coast. They pass Tarentum, Cape Lacinium, Caulon and Scylaceum, and sight Etna far off. Then the roar of broken water reaches them, and Anchises recognises Charybdis, of which Helenus had warned; the helmsman turns hard to the left, and the ships are lifted to heaven and dropped to the shades below, three times. The wind fails with the sun, and they drift ashore in the land of the Cyclopes. The harbour is calm, but Etna thunders beside it, throwing up black cloud, fire and molten rock, and (so the story goes) the giant Enceladus lies pinned beneath it, shifting his weary side. All night, hidden in the woods, they endure the portent and cannot see its cause. At dawn a wasted, ragged figure staggers out of the trees and stretches out his hands: a Greek who fought at Troy. Seeing Trojan dress and arms he hesitates in terror, then throws himself at their feet and begs to be taken anywhere, or killed by human hands if they will. Anchises gives him his right hand to steady him, and the man begins to speak.

sentences.t:
Provehimur pelago vicina Ceraunia iuxta,
unde iter Italiam cursusque brevissimus undis.
sentences.l:
We are carried forward over the sea, the neighbouring Ceraunian cliffs along,
whence a way to Italy and a course shortest for the waves.
sentences.i: We sail on across the open sea, close along the nearby Ceraunian cliffs, from where the road to Italy is shortest for ships.
sentences.n: A new paragraph, and the narrative returns after Helenus's farewell. 'Provehimur' is a passive in form but active in sense, 'we are carried forward', a common way for a sailor to say 'we sail'. 'vicina Ceraunia iuxta' — the preposition 'iuxta' ('close by') follows its noun, and 'vicina' agrees with 'Ceraunia': 'the nearby Ceraunian (rocks)'. These are the cliffs of Epirus, the narrowest crossing to Italy; hence the next line, 'unde iter Italiam cursusque brevissimus undis', where 'est' is understood ('whence there is a road to Italy'), 'Italiam' is the accusative of the place to which with no preposition, and 'undis' is a dative of reference, 'for the waves' (i.e. for ships on them). 'brevissimus' is a superlative.

sentences.t: Sol ruit interea et montes umbrantur opaci;
sentences.l: The sun rushes down meanwhile and the mountains are shaded dark;
sentences.i: Meanwhile the sun sinks swiftly, and the mountains darken into shadow;
sentences.n: 'ruit' is a vivid present tense, 'rushes down',; sunset is pictured as a headlong fall. 'umbrantur' is a present passive, 'are shaded'. 'opaci' agrees with 'montes', 'dark, shadowy'. The semicolon sets the evening scene before the beaching.

sentences.i: We stretch ourselves on the lap of the longed-for land beside the water, having drawn lots for the oars, and here and there on the dry beach we see to our bodies;
sentences.n: 'sternimur' is a passive used in a middle sense, 'we stretch ourselves out'. 'optatae gremio telluris' — 'gremio' is an ablative, 'on the lap, in the bosom' of the land, and 'optatae' ('desired, longed for') is a perfect passive participle used as an adjective: Italy is in sight at last, so the land feels like the goal. 'ad undam' — 'by the water'. 'sortiti remos' — 'sortiti' is the perfect participle of the deponent 'sortior' ('draw lots'), with an active meaning, 'having drawn lots' (the lots decided who would watch). 'passim' means 'here and there, scattered'. 'corpora curamus' — 'we care for the bodies', that is, we rest and eat. The semicolon sets aside what follows: sleep.

sentences.t: fessos sopor inrigat artus.
sentences.l: the weary limbs sleep soaks.
sentences.i: and sleep steeps our tired limbs.
sentences.n: 'fessos… artus' — 'artus' is an accusative plural in -us of 'artus' (fourth declension, 'limb'), and it is the object of 'inrigat', 'waters, soaks' (Greenough's spelling; the familiar form is 'irrigat'). The verb is a metaphor, sleep poured over the limbs like water; 'sopor' is the subject, 'deep sleep'. Note that 'fessos' and 'artus' frame the clause around its subject and verb.

sentences.t: Necdum orbem medium Nox horis acta subibat:
sentences.l: Not yet the middle circle Night, driven by the hours, was approaching:
sentences.i: Night, driven on by the hours, had not yet reached the middle of her round:
sentences.n: 'Necdum' is 'and not yet'. 'orbem medium… subibat' — 'subeo' means 'go under, come up to', here 'approach' the midpoint of the circle of night's course, its turning point. 'horis acta' — 'acta' is a perfect passive participle of 'ago' ('driven'), with 'horis' an ablative of means, 'by the Hours', the hours being pictured as driving her chariot. The imperfect 'subibat' sets the scene against which the next action happens: it was not yet midnight. The colon introduces what Palinurus does.

sentences.t:
haud segnis strato surgit Palinurus et omnis
explorat ventos, atque auribus aera captat;
sentences.l:
not sluggish rises from his strewn bed Palinurus and all
the winds he tests, and with his ears the air he catches;
sentences.i: Palinurus, not slow, gets up from his bed and tests every wind, catching the air with his ears;
sentences.n: 'Palinurus' is Aeneas's helmsman (the name will matter, for the god of sleep will take him in Book V). 'haud segnis' is a litotes ('not slow' for 'quick, ready'). 'strato' is a perfect passive participle used as a noun, 'from the spread (bed)'. 'omnis' is Greenough's spelling of the accusative plural 'omnes' (you'll see this constantly, as with 'montis'): it agrees with 'ventos', and the two words are split across the line-break, with the verb 'explorat' ('searches out, tests') between them. 'atque auribus aera captat' — 'aera' is a Greek accusative singular of 'aer', 'air'; the helmsman listens to the air as well as feeling it.

sentences.t:
sidera cuncta notat tacito labentia caelo,
Arcturum pluviasque Hyadas geminosque Triones,
armatumque auro circumspicit Oriona.
sentences.l:
all the stars he notes gliding in the silent sky,
Arcturus and the rainy Hyades and the twin Oxen,
and armed with gold he looks around at Orion.
sentences.i: He marks all the stars gliding through the silent sky: Arcturus, the rainy Hyades, the two Bears, and Orion, armed with gold, which he surveys on every side.
sentences.n: 'sidera cuncta notat… labentia' — 'labentia' is a present participle, neuter plural, 'gliding', agreeing with 'sidera'; 'tacito caelo' is an ablative of place where. A sailor steered by the stars, and he is here reading the weather by them. 'Arcturum' is the bright star in Boötes; 'pluviasque Hyadas' — the Hyades were a cluster whose rising was said to bring rain (the Greek name may be connected with the Greek for 'rain'), and 'Hyadas' is a Greek accusative plural. 'geminos Triones' — 'the twin ploughing-oxen', the Latin name for the Great and Little Bear, both seen circling the pole. 'armatum auro… Oriona' — Orion with his belt and sword, studded with gold stars, and 'Oriona' is another Greek accusative. The hyperbaton 'armatumque auro circumspicit Oriona' puts the epithet first and the name at the very end of the list and line.

sentences.t:
Postquam cuncta videt caelo constare sereno,
dat clarum e puppi signum;
sentences.l:
After all things he sees to stand firm in a clear sky,
he gives a clear signal from the stern;
sentences.i: When he sees that everything stands fixed in a cloudless sky, he gives a clear signal from the stern;
sentences.n: 'Postquam' ('after') with the present 'videt', where English would say 'had seen' or 'sees': Latin uses the present to give the sequence a quick vividness. 'cuncta… constare' — an accusative and infinitive after 'videt': 'he sees all things to stand firm', that is, the signs of weather are settled. 'caelo sereno' is an ablative of place (or circumstance). 'clarum… signum' — 'clarum' is both 'clear' and 'loud'; 'e puppi' — from the stern, where the helmsman stands.

sentences.t:
nos castra movemus,
temptamusque viam et velorum pandimus alas.
sentences.l:
we move camp, and make trial of the way
and spread the wings of sails.
sentences.i: we strike camp, try the road of the sea, and open the wings of the sails.
sentences.n: 'nos castra movemus' — a military phrase, 'we break camp'; the sailors treat the shore-camp as a soldier would. 'temptamusque viam' — 'tempto' is 'try, test', here try the course. The double '-que… et' links the two verbs with the last. 'velorum… alas' — 'alas' ('wings') as a metaphor for sails, with 'velorum' a genitive of definition ('the wings that are sails'). The tense is again the vivid present.

sentences.t:
Iamque rubescebat stellis Aurora fugatis,
cum procul obscuros collis humilemque videmus
Italiam.
sentences.l:
And now was growing red with stars put to flight Dawn,
when far off dim hills and low
Italy we see.
sentences.i: And now Dawn was reddening, the stars driven off, when from far away we see dim hills and Italy lying low.
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'Iamque rubescebat… cum… videmus' — the imperfect with 'iamque… cum' is a regular pattern for a sudden event (the 'inverted cum' clause), 'already X was happening, when Y'. 'stellis fugatis' is an ablative absolute, 'the stars having been put to flight'. 'obscuros collis humilemque… Italiam' — 'collis' is Greenough's accusative plural (the familiar form is 'colles'); 'obscuros' ('dim') belongs to the hills and 'humilem' ('low') to Italy; the word 'Italiam', delayed to the start of the next line, is the great reveal, and its position is the point of the sentence. It is the first sight of Italy in the poem.

sentences.t:
“Italiam ”primus conclamat Achates,
“Italiam ”laeto socii clamore salutant.
sentences.l:
“Italy ” first cries out Achates,
“Italy ” with glad shout the comrades hail.
sentences.i: “Italy!” cries Achates first of all; “Italy!” the comrades hail it with a joyful shout.
sentences.n: Greenough prints the marks oddly here (“Italiam ”primus: an opening mark, then the closing mark after a space); t is kept as printed, and the cries are marked correctly in l and i. 'Italiam' is an accusative of exclamation: no verb is needed. 'primus conclamat Achates' — 'primus' is an adjective used like an adverb, 'first'; Achates is Aeneas's faithful companion (the 'fidus Achates' of Book I), and he is the first to see. The word 'Italiam' is repeated in the next line, the anaphora giving the shout of a crowd. The verbs are 'conclamat' ('cries out together') and 'salutant' ('greet').

sentences.t:
Tum pater Anchises magnum cratera corona
induit, implevitque mero, divosque vocavit
stans celsa in puppi:
sentences.l:
Then father Anchises a great mixing-bowl with a garland
crowned, and filled it with unmixed wine, and the gods called on,
standing on the high stern:
sentences.i: Then father Anchises put a garland round a great mixing-bowl, filled it with wine, and called on the gods, standing on the high stern:
sentences.n: 'cratera' is a Greek accusative singular of 'crater', the bowl in which wine was mixed with water, here used for a libation. 'corona induit' — 'induo' means 'put on', so literally he 'clothed the bowl with a garland', with 'corona' an ablative of means. 'implevitque mero' — 'merum' is wine unmixed with water (a libation to the gods of the sea). 'divosque vocavit' — 'divos' is the accusative plural of 'divus', 'god' (Greenough keeps the old spelling with -o-; compare 'divom'). 'stans celsa in puppi' — the preposition 'in' is placed between its adjective and noun ('celsa in puppi'). The colon opens a prayer, which fills the next two lines.

sentences.t:
“Di maris et terrae tempestatumque potentes,
ferte viam vento facilem et spirate secundi.”
sentences.l:
“Gods of sea and land and of the tempests powerful,
carry the way easy with wind and breathe favourably.”
sentences.i: “Gods who rule the sea and the land and the storms, make the way easy with a wind, and blow kindly upon us.”
sentences.n: The prayer. 'Di maris et terrae tempestatumque potentes' — 'potentes' is a nominative (vocative) adjective with a genitive, 'powerful over the sea, the land and the tempests'; the genitive after an adjective of power is common. 'tempestatum' is a genitive plural. 'ferte viam vento facilem' — 'ferte' is the imperative of 'fero', 'bring, carry' (the gods are asked to make the way), 'vento' an ablative of means, and 'facilem' a predicate adjective, 'easy'. 'spirate secundi' — 'spirate' is an imperative; 'secundi' is a nominative plural adjective used as an adverb: 'blow favourably' (literally, 'following'), and a following wind is a fair wind. The closing mark ” ends Anchises's prayer.

sentences.t:
Crebrescunt optatae aurae portusque patescit
iam propior, templumque adparet in arce Minervae.
sentences.l:
Grow strong the longed-for breezes, and the harbour opens up,
now nearer, and a temple appears on the citadel of Minerva.
sentences.i: The breezes we prayed for freshen, the harbour opens out, now closer, and a temple of Minerva shows on the height.
sentences.n: 'Crebrescunt' is an inceptive verb ('grow thick, freshen'), and 'optatae aurae' ('the wished-for breezes') answers the prayer just made. 'portusque patescit iam propior' — 'patescit' is also inceptive ('lies open, comes into view'), and 'propior' is a comparative, 'nearer'. 'adparet' is Greenough's spelling for 'apparet' (the Latin Library prints it with 'pp'; a spelling difference only). 'templum… in arce Minervae' — the temple stands on a height on the Calabrian shore, traditionally near what is later Hydruntum (Otranto); Virgil names no place.

sentences.t: Vela legunt socii et proras ad litora torquent.
sentences.l: The sails gather in the comrades and the prows to the shores they turn.
sentences.i: The crew gather in the sails and turn the prows towards the beach.
sentences.n: 'Vela legunt' — 'lego' ('gather') is used in two senses, 'pick up' and 'furl', so 'they take in the sails'. 'proras ad litora torquent' — 'torqueo' is 'twist, turn'. The verbs are in the vivid present, and the two actions are listed without a link (asyndeton) to give the speed of the manoeuvre.

sentences.t:
Portus ab Euroo fluctu curvatus in arcum,
obiectae salsa spumant aspargine cautes;
sentences.l:
The harbour, from the eastern wave curved into a bow,
the rocks thrown against it foam with salt spray;
sentences.i: The harbour is bent into an arc by the eastern surge, and the rocks flung out before it foam with salt spray;
sentences.n: 'Portus ab Euroo fluctu curvatus in arcum' — 'curvatus' is a perfect passive participle, 'curved', with 'ab… fluctu' marking the agent, 'by the wave', and 'Euroo' is an adjective formed from 'Eurus', 'of the east wind', with a Greek-style ending, 'Eu-' being one syllable. 'obiectae… cautes' — 'obiectae' is a perfect passive participle, 'thrown in the way', so the rocks stand as a breakwater. 'salsa… aspargine' — Greenough's spelling of the ablative of 'aspargo' ('sprinkling, spray'); the Latin Library prints 'aspergine'. 'spumant' is a verb of the foam they make.

sentences.t: ipse latet;
sentences.l: itself lies hid;
sentences.i: the harbour itself is hidden;
sentences.n: 'ipse' is the harbour itself, behind the barrier of rocks: from the sea it is not visible. The unit is a small one and stands alone because of the semicolon on both sides.

sentences.t:
gemino demittunt bracchia muro
turriti scopuli, refugitque ab litore templum.
sentences.l:
with a twin wall let down their arms
the towered crags, and recedes from the shore the temple.
sentences.i: twin walls of towering crags reach out their arms, and the temple stands back from the beach.
sentences.n: 'gemino… muro' — an ablative of means, 'with a double wall'. 'demittunt bracchia' — 'bracchia' ('arms', Greenough's spelling) is a metaphor: the two arms of rock stretch down into the sea and embrace the harbour. 'turriti scopuli' — 'turriti' ('turreted, tower-like') agrees with 'scopuli' and is an adjective formed from 'turris'. 'refugitque ab litore templum' — 'refugio' means 'flee back', so the temple 'draws back' from the shore (it stands on the height).

sentences.t:
Quattuor hic, primum omen, equos in gramine vidi
tondentis campum late, candore nivali.
sentences.l:
Four here, a first omen, horses on the grass I saw
cropping the plain far and wide, in snowy whiteness.
sentences.i: Here, as a first omen, I saw four horses on the grass, cropping the plain far and wide, white as snow.
sentences.n: Here Aeneas himself narrates: this is still the first-person story told to Dido. 'primum omen' is in apposition to the whole sentence, 'as a first omen'. 'Quattuor… equos' is the object of 'vidi', with 'tondentis' (Greenough's accusative plural participle in -is, 'cropping', familiar as 'tondentes') agreeing; 'late' is an adverb, 'widely'. 'candore nivali' — an ablative of quality or description, 'with a snowy whiteness'. White horses are frequent in omens.

sentences.t:
Et pater Anchises: “Bellum, O terra hospita, portas
bello armantur equi, bellum haec armenta minantur.
sentences.l:
And father Anchises: “War, O hospitable land, you bring;
for war are armed horses, war these herds threaten.
sentences.i: And father Anchises said: “War, O welcoming land, is what you bring; horses are armed for war, and war is what these herds threaten.
sentences.n: The ellipsis of the verb of speaking ('Anchises said') is the pattern flagged before: 'Et pater Anchises:' and the quotation follows. The opening mark “ stands in the middle of the line. 'O terra hospita' is a vocative with a harsh joke in it: 'hospita' ('welcoming') is what the land ought to be. 'bellum… portas' — 'bellum' is placed first, emphatic. 'bello armantur equi' — 'bello' is an ablative of purpose or cause ('for war'), and 'armantur' is a passive: horses are 'armed' (harnessed) for war. 'haec armenta minantur' — 'haec armenta' ('these herds') is the subject; 'minantur' is the present of the deponent 'minor', 'threaten'. The anaphora of 'bellum… bello… bellum' stresses the word.

sentences.i: But still, these same four-footed creatures are used of old to submit to the chariot and to bear the harness in step beneath the yoke; there is hope of peace too,” he said.
sentences.n: 'Sed tamen' ('but yet') answers the first reading of the omen. 'idem' is neuter plural, agreeing with 'quadrupedes' (Greenough's spelling; the Latin Library prints 'quadripedes'), 'the same four-footed beasts'; 'sueti' is a contracted perfect passive participle of 'suesco', 'accustomed', and with the infinitives 'succedere' and 'ferre' it means 'accustomed to submit, to bear'. 'frena iugo concordia ferre' — 'concordia' ('in harmony, agreeing') is a neuter plural predicate, 'bear bridles agreeing under the yoke': horses in a team draw in step. 'spes et pacis' — 'est' is understood ('there is hope also of peace'). The closing mark ” stands before 'ait' in Greenough's print, as printed; the verb 'ait' ('he says') is the tag, and the speech ends at 'pacis'. Anchises thus reads the omen in two ways.

sentences.i: Then we pray to the holy divinity of Pallas of the clashing arms, who first welcomed us in our joy, and before the altars we veil our heads in the Phrygian cloak;
sentences.n: 'numina sancta' — the plural 'numina' for one goddess's divine power. 'Palladis armisonae' — 'armisonae' is a compound adjective, 'arms-sounding', from 'arma' and 'sono'; Pallas is the warrior-goddess; the Trojans treat her as the power of the place. 'quae prima accepit ovantis' — 'ovantis' is the accusative plural participle of 'ovo' ('exult'), agreeing with an understood 'nos'; Pallas was the first to receive them as they came ashore in joy. 'et capita ante aras Phrygio velamur amictu' — a passive in a middle sense, 'we veil ourselves', with 'capita' as a Greek-style accusative of respect ('as to our heads'). The covered head belongs to the sacrifice to Juno: Helenus had told them to veil their heads when they made it (3.403–407), so that no hostile face should break in on the rite.

sentences.t:
praeceptisque Heleni, dederat quae maxima, rite
Iunoni Argivae iussos adolemus honores.
sentences.l:
And by the instructions of Helenus, which he had given as the greatest, duly
to Argive Juno the bidden rites we burn.
sentences.i: And by the commands of Helenus, which he had set above all others, we duly burn the bidden offerings to Argive Juno.
sentences.n: 'praeceptisque Heleni, dederat quae maxima' — an ablative of means or accordance; 'dederat' is a pluperfect, and 'quae maxima' is a relative clause: the chief of his instructions, which was to win over Juno (3.437–440). 'Heleni' is a Greek genitive in -i. 'rite' means 'according to the proper rite'. 'Iunoni Argivae' — Juno was the goddess of Argos, the city of the Greeks, and in Virgil is the Trojans' enemy; 'Argivae' is an adjective with an ironic edge. 'iussos adolemus honores' — 'adoleo' is 'make to burn, burn in sacrifice', and 'honores' is 'the offerings', with 'iussos' ('commanded') a perfect passive participle.

sentences.t:
Haud mora, continuo perfectis ordine votis,
cornua velatarum obvertimus antemarum,
Graiugenumque domos suspectaque linquimus arva.
sentences.l:
No delay; immediately, the vows having been completed in order,
the horns of the sail-bearing yards we turn about,
and the homes of the Greek-born and the suspect fields we leave.
sentences.i: Without delay, as soon as the vows are fully paid, in due order, we swing about the ends of the sail-yards and leave the homes of the Greek-born and the fields we distrust.
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'Haud mora' has 'est' understood, 'there is no delay'. 'perfectis ordine votis' is an ablative absolute. 'cornua… antemarum' — the 'cornua' are the ends of the yard-arms; Greenough prints 'antemarum' (the Latin Library 'antemnarum'), a spelling of 'antemna', 'yard'. 'velatarum' is a perfect passive participle, 'sail-covered', agreeing with 'antemarum'. 'obvertimus' means 'turn towards', here 'turn about'. 'Graiugenum' is the old genitive plural in -um, 'of the Greek-born' (a compound adjective from 'Graius' and the root of 'gigno'); 'suspecta arva' — the Trojans fear the Greek colonies of southern Italy, which Helenus warned them to avoid.

sentences.t:
Hinc sinus Herculei (si vera est fama) Tarenti
cernitur;
sentences.l:
Hence the bay of Herculean (if true is the story) Tarentum
is seen;
sentences.i: From here the gulf of Tarentum, Hercules' city if the tale is true, comes into sight;
sentences.n: 'sinus Herculei… Tarenti' — Tarentum (modern Taranto) was a Spartan colony, but a legend made Hercules its founder; Virgil distances himself from the claim with the parenthesis '(si vera est fama)'. 'Herculei' agrees with 'Tarenti', which is a genitive. 'cernitur' is the passive of 'cerno', 'is seen, is made out'; the singular verb agrees with the nearest subject, 'sinus'.

sentences.t:
attollit se diva Lacinia contra,
Caulonisque arces et navifragum Scylaceum.
sentences.l:
rises up against it the goddess Lacinia,
and the citadels of Caulon and ship-wrecking Scylaceum.
sentences.i: opposite, the goddess of Lacinium lifts her temple, and Caulon's citadel and Scylaceum, the wrecker of ships.
sentences.n: 'attollit se diva Lacinia contra' — 'diva Lacinia' is Juno Lacinia, whose temple stood on the Lacinian headland, near Croton. 'contra' is an adverb, 'opposite'. 'Caulonisque arces' — 'Caulonis' is a genitive; Caulon (Caulonia) was a Greek town. 'navifragum Scylaceum' — 'navifragum' ('ship-breaking') is an adjective built from 'navis' and the root of 'frango'; the Greek town of that name stood on a rocky coast.

sentences.t:
Tum procul e fluctu Trinacria cernitur Aetna,
et gemitum ingentem pelagi pulsataque saxa
audimus longe fractasque ad litora voces,
sentences.l:
Then far off from the wave Sicilian Etna is seen,
and a groan huge of the sea and the beaten rocks
we hear from afar, and broken voices at the shores,
sentences.i: Then, far away beyond the waves, Sicilian Etna is seen, and from afar we hear the vast groan of the sea, the battered rocks, and the broken voices on the shores,
sentences.n: 'Trinacria Aetna' — 'Trinacria' is the island's Greek name, 'three-pointed', so 'Trinacrian Etna'. 'gemitum ingentem pelagi pulsataque saxa' — 'pulsata' ('beaten') is a perfect passive participle agreeing with 'saxa', and both 'gemitum' and 'saxa' are objects of 'audimus'. 'fractasque ad litora voces' — 'fractas' ('broken') voices are the sound of the surf; the preposition 'ad' is between its adjective phrase and noun. The comma at the end carries on to the next clause.

sentences.t: exsultantque vada, atque aestu miscentur harenae.
sentences.l: and the shallows leap up, and with the surge the sands are mingled.
sentences.i: and the shoals leap up, and the sands are churned with the swell.
sentences.n: 'exsultantque vada' — 'vada' are 'shallows, shoals', here the water over them. 'aestu miscentur harenae' — 'aestu' is an ablative of means, 'by the surge' (the word also means 'heat, tide'); 'miscentur' is a passive. The noise and the churning are signs of the whirlpool before Anchises names it.

sentences.t:
Et pater Anchises: “Nimirum haec illa Charybdis:
hos Helenus scopulos, haec saxa horrenda canebat.
sentences.l:
And father Anchises: “Surely this is that Charybdis:
these rocks Helenus, these dreadful crags was telling of.
sentences.i: And father Anchises: “Surely this is that Charybdis; Helenus told of these rocks, these terrible crags.
sentences.n: Again the ellipsis of the verb of speaking. 'Nimirum' ('doubtless, surely') begins a confident recognition. 'haec illa Charybdis' — 'haec' is the Greenough text; the Latin Library prints 'hic' ('this one'): the sense is the same. 'illa' means 'that famous'. Charybdis is the whirlpool opposite Scylla in the strait of Messina. 'hos Helenus scopulos, haec saxa horrenda canebat' — 'canebat' is the imperfect of 'cano', 'sing, foretell', 'was telling of', and it governs the accusatives 'scopulos' and 'saxa', put first for emphasis. 'horrenda' is a gerundive used as an adjective, 'to be shuddered at'. Helenus had actually described the strait to them before (3.410–432, in the last part).

sentences.t: Eripite, O socii, pariterque insurgite remis!”
sentences.l: Snatch us away, O comrades, and together rise to the oars!”
sentences.i: Pull us clear, comrades, and bend together to the oars!”
sentences.n: 'Eripite' — the imperative of 'eripio', 'snatch away', understood with 'nos' or 'navem' ('rescue us'): the sailors must pull the ships out of danger. 'insurgite remis' — 'insurgo' means 'rise to', so 'stand and heave on the oars', as rowers lean back with the full weight of the body, and 'remis' is a dative or an ablative of means. 'O socii' is a vocative. The closing mark ” ends Anchises's speech.

sentences.t:
Haud minus ac iussi faciunt, primusque rudentem
contorsit laevas proram Palinurus ad undas.
sentences.l:
No less than bidden they do, and first the creaking rope
wrenched to the left prow Palinurus towards the waves.
sentences.i: They do no less than they are told, and Palinurus is the first to wrench the groaning prow round to the waves on the left.
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'Haud minus ac iussi faciunt' — 'haud minus ac' ('no less than') and 'iussi' ('having been ordered') is a perfect participle used as a predicate, 'obedient'. 'primusque rudentem contorsit laevas proram Palinurus ad undas' — a long line with a clear hyperbaton: 'rudentem' ('creaking, groaning') belongs with 'proram', but the adjective comes first, 'laevas' ('left') belongs with 'undas', and 'Palinurus' is held back to the end of the line. 'rudens' as an adjective is a participle of 'rudo' ('roar, creak'), and 'contorsit' is the perfect of 'contorqueo', 'twist round'. The direction is to the left, as Helenus had advised (3.410–413).

sentences.t: laevam cuncta cohors remis ventisque petivit.
sentences.l: To the left all the company with oars and winds made for.
sentences.i: The whole company made for the left, with oars and with winds.
sentences.n: The line begins without a capital in Greenough's print, a quirk of the printing, not of sense. 'laevam' is the object of 'petivit', 'sought, made for', and 'cuncta cohors' — the whole crew — is the subject. 'cohors' is a word from the army: the company is a unit of soldiers. 'remis ventisque' — ablative of means, 'by oars and winds'.

sentences.t:
Tollimur in caelum curvato gurgite, et idem
subducta ad Manis imos desedimus unda.
sentences.l:
We are lifted up into the sky on the curved eddy, and the same
with the wave drawn away to the lowest shades we sank down.
sentences.i: We are lifted up to the sky on the arching whirl, and, the wave drawn back from under us, we sink down again to the deepest shades.
sentences.n: 'curvato gurgite' — an ablative of means or absolute, 'with the whirl curved' into a heaving arch. 'idem' agrees with the subject 'nos', 'we, the very same (people)', in a sentence with a sharp contrast between rising and falling. 'subducta ad Manis imos desedimus unda' — 'subducta unda' is an ablative absolute, 'the wave having been drawn away from beneath'. 'Manis' is Greenough's spelling of the accusative plural 'Manes', the spirits of the dead, and 'imos' means 'the lowest', so 'to the lowest ghosts' — the underworld. 'desedimus' is the perfect of 'desido', 'sink down'.

sentences.t: Ter scopuli clamorem inter cava saxa dedere:
sentences.l: Thrice the crags a roar among the hollow rocks gave:
sentences.i: Three times the crags gave out a roar among their hollow rocks;
sentences.n: 'dedere' is the perfect third person plural, 'dedērunt' contracted: an '-ere' ending standing for '-erunt' (flagged in the first part, and you'll see it constantly). 'clamorem inter cava saxa' — the preposition 'inter' stands after its noun phrase's first word ('clamorem inter'), and 'cava saxa' are the hollow caves in the cliffs. The colon leads into the matching line that follows.

sentences.t: ter spumam elisam et rorantia vidimus astra.
sentences.l: thrice the spray flung up and the dripping stars we saw.
sentences.i: three times we saw the spray thrown up and the stars dripping wet.
sentences.n: 'ter' repeats the 'ter' of the previous line, an anaphora. 'spumam elisam' — 'elisam' is a perfect passive participle of 'elido' ('dash out, strike out'), 'spray dashed up'. 'rorantia… astra' — the stars appear to drip with 'ros' ('dew'): the spray has flown so high that it seems to reach and wet the sky. This is a hyperbole; Charybdis and her whirlpool are Homer's, from Odyssey 12.

sentences.t:
Interea fessos ventus cum sole reliquit,
ignarique viae Cyclopum adlabimur oris.
sentences.l:
Meanwhile the weary the wind with the sun left,
and, ignorant of the way, we glide to the shores of the Cyclopes.
sentences.i: Meanwhile the wind left us weary along with the sun, and, not knowing the way, we drift on to the Cyclopes' shores.
sentences.n: 'fessos' is the object of 'reliquit', 'the weary (crew)'. 'cum sole' — the wind fell with the sunset. 'ignari viae' — a genitive after an adjective of knowing, 'ignorant of the way'; 'ignarique' is a nominative plural adjective, agreeing with 'nos'. 'Cyclopum' is the old genitive plural in -um (you'll see this constantly); 'adlabimur' ('glide to') takes the dative 'oris'. After the strait, the ships have been carried round to the east coast of Sicily.

sentences.t:
Portus ab accessu ventorum immotus et ingens
ipse;
sentences.l:
A harbour from the approach of the winds undisturbed and vast
itself;
sentences.i: The harbour is untroubled by any approach of winds, and vast;
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'Portus ab accessu ventorum immotus et ingens ipse' — 'ab accessu' ('from the approach') gives the source of danger, 'immotus' ('unmoved, undisturbed') and 'ingens' are predicate adjectives, and 'ipse' is the harbour 'itself', in contrast with what lies beside it. The word 'ipse' is delayed to the next line to prepare the contrast with Etna: the harbour is still, but the mountain beside it is not.

sentences.t: sed horrificis iuxta tonat Aetna ruinis;
sentences.l: but with dreadful crashings close by thunders Etna;
sentences.i: but close beside it Etna thunders with terrifying upheavals;
sentences.n: 'sed horrificis iuxta tonat Aetna ruinis' — 'iuxta' is an adverb here, 'close by', and 'horrificis… ruinis' is an ablative of manner, 'with terrifying collapses' (from the mountain's inner fall and the rocks thrown out). 'tonat' is a present of 'tono', 'thunder'. The 'sed' turns from the calm harbour to the active volcano.

sentences.i: and at times it bursts forth a black cloud into the upper air, smoking with a pitch-black whirlwind and white-hot cinders, and lifts balls of flame and licks the stars;
sentences.n: 'interdum… interdum' — 'at times… at times' (the second at 575) divides the volcano's behaviour into two kinds. 'atram prorumpit ad aethera nubem' — 'prorumpit' is a transitive 'bursts forth', with 'nubem' its object, 'atram' ('black') split from it, and 'ad aethera' is a Greek-style accusative ('aethera') of the upper air. 'turbine fumantem piceo et candente favilla' — 'fumantem' agrees with 'nubem', 'smoking', with two ablatives: 'turbine piceo' ('with a pitchy whirlwind') and 'favilla candente' ('with glowing ash'); 'candente' is the present participle of 'candeo', 'glow white-hot'. 'attollitque globos flammarum' — the genitive plural 'flammarum' with 'globos'. 'sidera lambit' — the licking of the stars by the flames: an exaggeration.

sentences.t:
interdum scopulos avolsaque viscera montis
erigit eructans, liquefactaque saxa sub auras
cum gemitu glomerat, fundoque exaestuat imo.
sentences.l:
at times rocks and the torn-away entrails of the mountain
it hurls up, belching, and melted stones into the air
with a groan it rolls together, and from its lowest depth boils up.
sentences.i: At times it throws up crags and the torn entrails of the mountain, belching them out, and heaps molten rock into the air with a groan, and seethes from its lowest depth.
sentences.n: 'avolsaque viscera montis' — 'avolsa' is Greenough's spelling of the perfect passive participle of 'avello' ('tear away'); the Latin Library prints 'auulsa' — orthography only. 'viscera' ('entrails') is the mountain's inner body, a human metaphor. 'erigit eructans' — 'eructo' means 'belch out', so 'raises, belching'. 'liquefacta saxa' — 'liquefacta' ('made liquid') is a perfect participle, 'melted stones'. 'sub auras' — 'sub' with the accusative of motion, 'up into the airs'. 'glomerat' ('rolls into a ball, heaps') and 'exaestuat' ('boils up') are vivid presents; 'fundo… imo' is an ablative of the place from which.

sentences.i: There is a tale that the body of Enceladus, half-burned by the thunderbolt, is pinned beneath this mass, and that huge Etna, laid upon him, breathes out flame from burst furnaces;
sentences.n: 'Fama est' introduces an accusative and infinitive: 'corpus… urgueri' (the old passive infinitive of 'urgeo', Greenough's spelling; the Latin Library 'urgeri'), 'ingentem Aetnam impositam… exspirare', 'the body to be pressed… Etna, laid on it, to breathe out'. Enceladus was one of the Giants who fought the gods; Jupiter's bolt struck him and Etna was put on top of him to hold him down. 'semustum' means 'half-burnt'. 'mole hac' is an ablative of means. 'ruptis… caminis' is an ablative of source, 'from broken furnaces'; 'caminus' is a smelting-furnace, so volcanoes were a smithy of the gods. 'insuper' ('on top') is an adverb.

sentences.t:
et fessum quotiens mutet latus, intremere omnem
murmure Trinacriam, et caelum subtexere fumo.
sentences.l:
and as often as he changes his weary side, to tremble all
with a rumble Trinacria, and the sky to be veiled with smoke.
sentences.i: and that whenever he shifts his tired side the whole of Sicily trembles with a rumbling, and the sky is veiled in smoke.
sentences.n: The infinitives continue under 'Fama est': 'intremere omnem… Trinacriam', 'et caelum subtexere fumo'. 'quotiens mutet' — 'quotiens' ('as often as') with a present subjunctive: the subjunctive is used because the clause is part of the reported statement. 'fessum… latus' — Enceladus turns from one side to the other, and each turn causes an earthquake. 'omnem' is the accusative singular, agreeing with 'Trinacriam'. 'subtexere' means 'weave beneath', so the smoke spreads like a woven veil beneath the sky.

sentences.t:
Noctem illam tecti silvis immania monstra
perferimus, nec quae sonitum det causa videmus.
sentences.l:
That night, hidden in the woods, the monstrous marvels
we endure, and what the cause gives the sound we do not see.
sentences.i: All that night, sheltered in the woods, we endure the monstrous wonders, and we cannot see what cause makes the sound.
sentences.n: 'Noctem illam' is an accusative of duration, 'for that night'. 'tecti silvis' — 'tecti' is a perfect passive participle, 'covered', with 'silvis' an ablative of means. 'immania monstra' — 'monstra' are portents, here the volcano's wonders. 'perferimus' means 'endure to the end'. 'nec quae sonitum det causa videmus' — an indirect question with the subjunctive 'det': 'quae… causa' ('what cause') is placed in the middle of its clause, the verb 'det' ('gives, produces') coming before its subject, which is a hyperbaton.

sentences.t:
Nam neque erant astrorum ignes, nec lucidus aethra
siderea polus, obscuro sed nubila caelo,
et lunam in nimbo nox intempesta tenebat.
sentences.l:
For neither were there the fires of the stars, nor bright with ether
starry the sky, but clouds in a dark heaven,
and the moon in a cloud-bank the dead of night held.
sentences.i: For there were no fires of stars, no sky bright with starry air, but cloud in a darkened heaven, and the dead of night held the moon in a rain-cloud.
sentences.n: 'Nam neque erant astrorum ignes' — the stars are called 'fires'. 'nec lucidus aethra siderea polus' — 'aethra' is an ablative of cause or means ('with the starry ether'), 'siderea' agrees with 'aethra', and 'lucidus… polus' is the subject. 'lucidus' and 'polus' frame the phrase between them: 'bright… sky', with the starry ether in the middle. 'obscuro sed nubila caelo' — 'nubila' ('clouds') is a neuter plural noun, with the verb 'erant' understood. 'lunam in nimbo' — the moon is 'in' (shut up in) a rain-cloud. 'nox intempesta' — the 'unseasonable' (dead) of night, the middle of it, a fixed phrase; 'tenebat' means 'held, kept hidden'.

sentences.t:
Postera iamque dies primo surgebat Eoo,
umentemque Aurora polo dimoverat umbram:
sentences.l:
The next day and now was rising with the first Dawn-star,
and the damp shadow from the sky Aurora had driven away:
sentences.i: And now the next day was rising with the first light of the east, and Dawn had swept the dank shadow from the sky;
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'Postera… dies' ('the following day') is a nominative, and the 'iamque… cum' pattern again sets the sudden event of the next lines against the dawn. 'primo Eoo' — 'Eous' is the morning star or the east; the ablative with 'primo' marks the time. 'umentem… umbram' (Greenough's spelling of 'umidam') is 'damp shadow' with 'polo' an ablative of separation, 'from the sky'. 'dimoverat' is a pluperfect, 'had driven off'. The colon opens the entrance of a figure.

sentences.t:
cum subito e silvis, macie confecta suprema,
ignoti nova forma viri miserandaque cultu
procedit, supplexque manus ad litora tendit.
sentences.l:
when suddenly from the woods, with lean wasting to the utmost worn out,
of an unknown man a strange shape and pitiable in dress
advances, and suppliant his hands to the shore holds out.
sentences.i: when suddenly from the woods there comes out, worn to the last degree of leanness, the strange form of an unknown man, pitiable in his clothing, and, begging, he holds out his hands to the shore.
sentences.n: 'cum subito' — the second half of the 'iamque… cum' sentence. 'macie confecta suprema' — 'confecta' ('worn out') is a perfect passive participle agreeing with 'forma', and 'macie… suprema' is an ablative of cause, 'by extreme leanness' (note the adjective placed after, with the noun). 'ignoti nova forma viri' — 'nova' means 'strange, unusual'; the genitive 'ignoti viri' is separated from 'forma' by the adjective. 'miserandaque cultu' — 'miseranda' is a gerundive, 'to be pitied', and 'cultu' is an ablative of respect, 'in dress'. 'supplexque manus ad litora tendit' — a gesture of prayer, with 'supplex' as a predicate nominative.

sentences.t: Respicimus:
sentences.l: We look back:
sentences.i: We turn and look:
sentences.n: 'Respicimus' means 'we look back (or at)', the crew turning to see. The colon announces a description of the man in the next lines.

sentences.t:
dira inluvies inmissaque barba,
consertum tegumen spinis;
sentences.l:
dreadful filth and a hanging beard,
a garment fastened together with thorns;
sentences.i: horrible filth, a beard grown long and untended, a covering pinned together with thorns;
sentences.n: 'dira inluvies' — 'inluvies' (Greenough's spelling; the familiar 'illuvies') is a nominative, 'filth'. 'inmissa barba' — 'inmissa' ('let loose'; the Latin Library prints 'immissa') is a perfect passive participle, 'long and uncut'. 'consertum tegumen spinis' — 'consertum' is a perfect participle of 'consero', 'fasten together', agreeing with the neuter 'tegumen' ('covering', Greenough's spelling; the Latin Library 'tegimen'), with 'spinis' an ablative of means. There is no verb in the list: the description is a series of nominatives, a pause in the narrative.

sentences.t:
at cetera Graius,
[et quondam patriis ad Troiam missus in armis.]
sentences.l:
but in all else a Greek,
[and once to Troy sent in his country's arms.]
sentences.i: though in everything else he was a Greek, [and once was sent to Troy in the arms of his homeland.]
sentences.n: 'at cetera Graius' — 'cetera' is an accusative of respect, 'in the rest', and 'Graius' is a nominative adjective, 'Greek'. Line 595 is printed in square brackets by Greenough as a spurious line (a line he thinks was not written by Virgil, one of 61 he marks); it is kept here and read with the rest. 'quondam patriis ad Troiam missus in armis' — 'missus' is a perfect passive participle, 'sent', 'in armis' means 'in arms', and 'patriis' ('his country's') is an adjective. The man's story follows in the next part.

sentences.i: And when he saw Dardanian dress and Trojan arms in the distance, he halted, a little terrified at the sight, and held back his step;
sentences.n: 'Isque' = 'et is'. 'Dardanios habitus et Troia… arma' — 'Dardanios' and 'Troia' are adjectives ('Dardanian', 'Trojan'): 'Dardania' is the land of Dardanus, Troy's founder. 'habitus' is an accusative plural of the fourth declension. The word 'procul' ('from afar') belongs with 'vidit', and 'Troia' and 'arma' are split across the line, with the verb in the middle. 'paulum aspectu conterritus haesit' — 'paulum' is an adverb ('a little'), 'aspectu' an ablative of cause, 'conterritus' a perfect passive participle, 'haesit' means 'stuck, hung back'. 'continuitque gradum' — 'continuit' is 'held back'.

sentences.t:
mox sese ad litora praeceps
cum fletu precibusque tulit:
sentences.l:
then himself to the shores headlong
with weeping and prayers he carried:
sentences.i: then, headlong, he flung himself down to the shore in tears and with prayers:
sentences.n: 'mox' ('then, soon after') shows his fear is overcome by the need. 'sese… tulit' — 'se ferre' is 'to carry oneself, rush'; 'sese' is the emphatic form of 'se'. 'praeceps' is a nominative adjective, 'headlong', used as an adverb. 'cum fletu precibusque' — the preposition 'cum' stands with the first of two ablatives. The colon opens his speech.

sentences.i: “By the stars I call you to witness, by the gods above and by this breathable light of heaven: take me, Trojans;
sentences.n: The castaway's speech. 'Per sidera testor' — 'testor' is a deponent, 'I call to witness', and 'per' with the accusative introduces what he swears by (an oath of supplication); the preposition is repeated at 600, 'per superos', 'by the gods above'. 'hoc caeli spirabile lumen' — 'spirabile' ('that can be breathed') is a rare adjective, so the light is thought of as air, and 'caeli' is a genitive, 'of heaven'. 'tollite me' — 'tollo' ('lift') is here 'take up, take aboard'. 'Teucri' is a vocative, 'Trojans' (the descendants of Teucer). The opening mark “ begins the speech.

sentences.t: quascumque abducite terras;
sentences.l: to whatever lands carry me away;
sentences.i: carry me off to whatever lands you will;
sentences.n: 'quascumque abducite terras' — 'quascumque' is a relative ('whichever') agreeing with 'terras', here an accusative of the place to which with no preposition, 'to whatever lands'. 'abducite' is an imperative ('carry away'). The hyperbaton puts the indefinite relative before the verb as a gesture of desperation: any land at all.

sentences.t: hoc sat erit.
sentences.l: this will be enough.
sentences.i: that will be enough.
sentences.n: 'hoc sat erit' — 'sat' is the short form of 'satis' (enough), and 'hoc' refers to being taken away from the island. The three short words close the request.

sentences.t:
Scio me Danais e classibus unum,
et bello Iliacos fateor petiisse Penatis;
sentences.l:
I know myself, from the Danaan fleet one,
and in war I confess that I attacked the Trojan Penates;
sentences.i: I know that I am one of the Danaan fleet, and I admit that I made war on the household gods of Troy;
sentences.n: 'Scio me… unum' — 'scio' takes an accusative and infinitive with 'esse' understood, 'I know myself to be one'. 'Danais e classibus' — 'Danais' is an adjective in this phrase (Danaan), 'classibus' an ablative plural; the two words flank the preposition 'e'. 'bello Iliacos fateor petiisse Penatis' — 'petiisse' is a perfect infinitive of 'peto', 'to have attacked'; 'Penatis' is Greenough's accusative plural in -is for 'Penates', the household gods of a family or city. 'Iliacos' is an adjective from 'Ilium', 'of Ilium', that is, Troy. He admits his guilt to disarm them.

sentences.t:
pro quo, si sceleris tanta est iniuria nostri,
spargite me in fluctus, vastoque inmergite ponto.
sentences.l:
for which, if so great is the wrong of our crime,
scatter me into the waves, and plunge me in the vast sea.
sentences.i: For that, if the wrong of our crime is so great, scatter me into the waves and plunge me in the boundless sea.
sentences.n: 'pro quo' — 'for which', a connecting relative (flagged in the first part) with 'pro' meaning 'in return for'. 'si sceleris tanta est iniuria nostri' — 'iniuria' ('wrong, injury') is the subject, with the genitive 'sceleris… nostri' ('of our crime'); the word 'nostri' is the genitive of 'noster', agreeing with 'sceleris'. The conditional is open. 'spargite me in fluctus' — 'spargo' is 'scatter', so tear him limb from limb. 'vastoque inmergite ponto' — 'inmergite' (Greenough's spelling; the Latin Library 'immergite'), 'plunge'; 'ponto' is dative or ablative with the compound verb. The two imperatives are offered as an alternative to rescue.

sentences.t: Si pereo, hominum manibus periisse iuvabit.”
sentences.l: If I perish, by the hands of men to have perished will please.”
sentences.i: If I must die, it will be a joy to have died at the hands of men.”
sentences.n: 'Si pereo' — the present tense for a future condition, giving the situation vividly. 'hominum manibus periisse iuvabit' — 'iuvabit' is an impersonal future, 'it will please', with the perfect infinitive 'periisse' as subject ('to have perished'); the construction is like that at 1.203 ('forsan et haec olim meminisse iuvabit'). 'hominum manibus' — the 'hands of men' stands against the sea and monsters of the previous line. The closing mark ” ends his speech.

sentences.t:
Dixerat, et genua amplexus genibusque volutans
haerebat.
sentences.l:
He had spoken, and the knees having embraced and at the knees rolling
he clung.
sentences.i: He had spoken, and, clasping our knees and grovelling at them, he clung on.
sentences.n: 'Dixerat' is a pluperfect, 'had spoken', a standard way of closing a speech. 'genua amplexus genibusque volutans' — 'amplexus' is the perfect participle of the deponent 'amplector', which has an active meaning, 'having embraced'; 'volutans' ('rolling') is a present participle, and the verb 'volvo' is used with a reflexive sense, 'rolling himself'. The forms 'genua' and 'genibus' (two cases of the same word) make a play. 'haerebat' is an imperfect, 'was clinging', a drawn-out action.

sentences.t:
Qui sit, fari, quo sanguine cretus,
hortamur;
sentences.l:
Who he might be, to tell, from what blood sprung,
we urge;
sentences.i: We urge him to tell us who he is and from what blood he is sprung;
sentences.n: 'hortamur' takes an infinitive ('fari') where Latin prose would use 'ut' and a subjunctive; this poetic construction is common in Virgil. 'Qui sit' is an indirect question with the subjunctive, 'who he is', and 'quo sanguine cretus' — 'cretus' is the perfect participle of 'cresco', 'sprung', with 'sanguine' an ablative of origin. The words 'fari' ('to speak') and 'cretus' are in a series of clauses without links.

sentences.t: quae deinde agitet fortuna, fateri.
sentences.l: what next may harass fortune, to confess.
sentences.i: and to confess what fortune now plagues him.
sentences.n: 'quae deinde agitet fortuna' — another indirect question, 'agitet' ('harasses') is subjunctive; the verb 'fateri' ('to confess') depends on 'hortamur' as 'fari' did. The word order of 'quae… fortuna' puts the relative adjective before the subject. 'deinde' means 'next, now'.

sentences.t:
Ipse pater dextram Anchises, haud multa moratus,
dat iuveni, atque animum praesenti pignore firmat.
sentences.l:
Himself the father Anchises his right hand, not much delaying,
gives to the young man, and his spirit with the present pledge strengthens.
sentences.i: Father Anchises himself gives his right hand to the young man without much delay, and steadies his spirit with the pledge there and then.
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'Ipse pater… Anchises' — 'ipse' means that the old man acts himself, without waiting for Aeneas. 'dextram' (understood 'manum') is the object of 'dat'. 'haud multa moratus' — 'moratus' is a perfect participle of the deponent 'moror', 'having delayed', with an active sense; 'multa' is a neuter accusative used as an adverb. 'iuveni' is a dative of the indirect object. 'praesenti pignore' — an ablative of means, 'with a present pledge' (the handshake), in which 'praesenti' means 'at hand, immediate'. The giving of the right hand is a Roman pledge of good faith.

sentences.t: Ille haec, deposita tandem formidine, fatur:
sentences.l: He these things, set aside at last the fear, says:
sentences.i: Having put aside his fear at last, he speaks as follows:
sentences.n: 'Ille' is the stranger, 'haec' ('these things') the words that will follow. 'deposita tandem formidine' — an ablative absolute, 'the fear having been laid down at last'. 'fatur' is the present of the deponent 'for', 'speak'. The colon opens his tale, which continues in the next part. This is the last line of the part.
